reason: The cited evidence (E1, E2) only generally states that laser cladding is useful for surface modification and that a specific HEA coating shows good wear resistance on H13 steel. It does not provide specific support for the key premises about hot-cracking mechanisms, microstructural refinement, or comparative fatigue/wear performance versus fusion welding.
premises: Laser cladding reduces hot-cracking risk by minimizing time in the critical temperature range for segregation of low-melting phases.
Laser cladding produces a refined microstructure with reduced segregation of crack-promoting phases.
Laser cladding can deposit a tailored repair coating (e.g., high-entropy alloy or nickel-based alloy) that restores surface integrity.
The repaired component will have comparable or better fatigue and wear properties than a fusion-welded repair.
The proposed coating material (e.g., FeCrNiTiZr HEA) is suitable as a repair material for hot-working tool steel.
